metadata.title: Financial Risk Classification using AI
metadata.note: STEM/AI topic-of-interest video, based on the author's own project: 'Automated Financial Document Risk Classification and Clause Detection.' Reframed around the paper's actual stated objective (per its own Impact Statement): can AI help flag financial risk and catch important legal clauses at a scale manual review can't match, as an assistive decision-support tool, not a replacement for professional judgment. Task 1: Hierarchical BiLSTM on SEC 10-K/10-Q risk classification (95.2% macro-F1, +10.9 over TF-IDF baseline, 116 filings from 15 companies). Task 2: LegalBERT fine-tuned for clause detection on CUAD (80.1% macro-F1 vs 77.6% TF-IDF baseline, using only 5% of training data — with an honest and important limitation: a 43.3% miss rate on present clauses). Built using the same proven pattern set as prior videos: folderLabel set explicitly on ClaudeComposerAsk beats (@HumanitariansAI), OutroCTA used instead of ClaudeTitleOutro, BLUF lines kept short to avoid edge-bleed, no stale sparse_by_design flags except the legitimate BrutalistHesitantWriter typing-beat exemption.

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk — HAI persona, world-language hello (short form only)
beats.narration_text: Hi. Can AI actually help catch financial risk and legal clauses at a scale no human team could manually review?

props.command: claude "flag financial risk levels and legal clauses across a large set of SEC filings and contracts, to help a human review team prioritize"

beats.role_note: MANDATORY — BrutalistHesitantWriter, executive summary, hesitation = the pedagogy
beats.narration_text: Here's the idea. AI can scan filings and contracts far faster than any human team. That sounds like a reason to let it replace manual review entirely. It isn't — it's built to assist that review, flagging what needs a human's attention first, not replacing the human who decides.

props.text:
AI can scan filings and contracts fast.
That sounds like a reason to replace review.
It isn't. It's built to assist, not replace.

qc.sparse_reason: hesitant-writer typing bookend accumulates one line token by token — mid-beat frames are mostly cream by design (documented exemption case in final_frame_check.py)

beats.role_note: vox-style illustration (C2/C3), NOT a build-loop beat
beats.narration_text: There are two real bottlenecks here. SEC filings can run fourteen thousand words, with risk buried inside dense legal language. Contracts can hide any of forty one different clause types, each with real financial and legal weight. Manual review of either, at scale, doesn't hold up.
beats.visual_intent: two cards showing the scale problem in each domain

beats.act: THE REAL PROBLEM — why this needs help, not automation
beats.visual_intent: simple description card framing the scale problem and the assistive goal
beats.narration_text: Every public company has to disclose risk in its filings. Every contract can hide clauses that matter financially and legally. Reviewing all of it by hand doesn't scale. The goal isn't to remove the human from that review — it's to flag what deserves their attention first.

lines: Every public company must disclose risk.
Every contract can hide dozens of clause types.
Manual review at this volume doesn't scale.
The goal: flag it for a human, not replace them.

beats.act: THE PIPELINE — how the flagging actually works
beats.narration_text: As a pipeline: raw filings and contracts go in. Key sections get extracted. A model classifies risk level. A second model detects legal clauses. Everything flagged gets routed to a human reviewer — the output is a shortlist to check, not an automated final decision.
beats.visual_intent: four-stage flow diagram ending at a human reviewer, not a final verdict

props.title: AI Flags It, a Human Decides
props.footerNote: the output is a flagged shortlist, not a final decision
props.sparkLine: AI narrows it down. A human decides.

beats.role_note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: UI appears because the interface IS the subject here
beats.narration_text: Here's what the system actually catches. On risk classification, it correctly flagged risk level with ninety five point two percent macro-F1 — well above a simple keyword baseline. On clause detection, it caught eighty point one percent macro-F1, even trained on just a small fraction of the available data.
beats.visual_intent: verdict artifact page with both task results, framed as catch rate not final judgment

items.label: Clause Detection
items.sub: 80.1% F1, even with limited training data

beats.role_note: the lesson, honest about scope — this is where the real limitation lives
beats.narration_text: But here's the catch that matters most. The system still missed forty three percent of the clauses that were actually present in the contracts. In a legal document, a missed clause isn't a minor error — it can carry real consequences. That's exactly why this stays a tool that assists a human reviewer, not one that replaces them.

lines: It still missed 43% of real clauses present.
A missed clause can carry real consequences.
That's why a human still reviews every flag.
This assists review — it does not replace it.
